Effects of Losing Medicaid on Body Weight and Health Behaviors (Job Market Paper)

Approximately 170,000 childless adults abruptly lost Medicaid coverage as a result of Tennessee’s 2005 Medicaid reform. Leveraging this policy-induced variation in health insurance coverage, I investigate the impact of large-scale Medicaid disenrollment on body weight and health behaviors. Using Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) data from 1997 to 2010, I estimate synthetic difference-in-differences models that compare Tennessee’s outcomes before and after the reform with those of a data-driven, synthetic Tennessee. The findings indicate that the reform increased Body Mass Index (BMI) among Tennessean childless adults by 0.37 points, contributing to roughly 4% rise in the prevalence of overweight or obese individuals (BMI≥25). The effects are strong among young (aged 20-39) as well as female childless adults, who likely experienced disproportionately large coverage loss due to the reform. Examining potential mechanisms, I find that decreased participation in moderate physical activity (e.g., cycling, swimming) and dietary changes partially explain the weight gain.

text:
Working papers

The Effects of Capped Piece-Rate Teacher Bonuses: Evidence from Advanced Placement — Paper, EdWorkingPaper 26-1456.



Abstract


I study a North Carolina program that paid AP teachers for each student earning a qualifying exam score, subject to a cap. Using student-course administrative records and within- and across-teacher variation, I find gains in credit-eligible AP scores. The distribution of gains offers little evidence that teachers shifted effort away from high-achieving students. Responses varied with the strength of the incentive and the nature of the teaching task.





Public Health Insurance and Employment Lock: Resolving the TennCare Puzzle — Paper, under review.



Abstract


Prior evaluations of Tennessee’s 2005 Medicaid disenrollment reach conflicting conclusions about employment. I revisit the question by distinguishing jobs that could offer employer-sponsored insurance from self-employment. Wage employment rose among older, less-educated childless adults, the group for whom health risk and loss of insurance were especially salient. The pattern is consistent with employment lock as a labor supply response to coverage loss.

Removing Barriers to College Credits: Where and for Whom AP Exam Fee Waivers Work — Paper, Economics of Education Review (accepted). Media coverage.

with M. Cade Lawson




Abstract


Using North Carolina student-course administrative records, we estimate how a statewide AP exam fee waiver affected exam participation and scores eligible for college credit. Exam participation rose by 2.1 percentage points. Average gains in credit-eligible scores were small, but the rate increased by about 3 percentage points among low-SES enrollees. A complementary analysis finds the largest responses in courses with the lowest predicted exam-taking propensity before the waiver.





Medicaid and Health Resilience: Evidence from TennCare Disenrollment — Journal version, Economics & Human Biology, 2026.



Abstract


I examine whether Medicaid protects people from the functional consequences of adverse health. Tennessee’s 2005 disenrollment provides a setting to compare childless adults before and after coverage loss. Uninsurance and poor self-rated health rose. Days of incapacitation also increased, while the frequency of physical and mental unhealthy days changed little. The findings suggest that access to insurance and affordable care can help preserve health resilience.
